records.name: Nigeria
records.summary:
Nigeria is among the most severe environments for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct is criminalised nationally under the SSMPA (14 years, applies to all including tourists), and 12 northern states apply Sharia law with the death penalty for male same-sex conduct. A transgender TikToker known as "Abuja Area Mama" was found beaten and dead on a highway in Abuja; police misgendered her in death and, six months later, no one has been arrested. Police have beaten LGBTQ+ people for "looking gay" — the SSMPA has been described as a "weaponised" law — and dating-app "kito" gangs use Grindr to lure victims into assault and robbery. The UK Foreign Office has warned LGBT+ travellers to Nigeria of arrest, violence, and death-penalty risks.

A proposed cross-dressing ban (not yet passed) would criminalise gender expression in public. Trans identity is NOT explicitly criminalized nationally (the SSMPA targets same-sex conduct), and the violence concentrates against local communities rather than tourists. sources.summary: BBC (Aug 2024): the beaten body of Abujan trans TikToker 'Abuja Area Mama', a 33-year-old transgender woman, was found on a highway in Abuja hours after she posted about visiting her boyfriend; police said preliminary investigations showed 'a man fully dressed in female clothing' and the Abuja police chief ordered a 'thorough and discreet' investigation. For this record: a documented trans-specific killing with official misgendering of the victim.

The Dial (Feb 2025): six months after Abuja Area Mama's killing, no suspects had been charged despite the announced investigation; Nigeria has no legal protections for LGBTQ+ people and the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 reinforced colonial-era criminalisation. For this record: impunity is documented — police response to a trans victim's killing produced no arrests half a year on.

Sahara Reporters (Aug 2026), reporting the latest UK FCDO travel advice for Nigeria: LGBT+ travellers warned of attacks, blackmail and intimidation, up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, and death-penalty risk under Sharia law in northern states. For this record: current (2026) official foreign-office warning aimed squarely at LGBT+ visitors.

TimesLIVE (Mar 2025): a 24-year-old man, Okafor, was stopped by Lagos police, struck in the mouth with a police gun butt and freed only after paying almost half of the 50,000 naira bribe demanded, for 'looking gay'; the SSMPA is described by those affected as a 'weaponised' law creating a climate of hostility. For this record: police extortion and violence against perceived-gay people, with the specific bribe amount and injury.

Context/Thomson Reuters Foundation (Aug 2024), marking 10 years of the SSMPA: the 2014 law has fuelled violence, extortion and discrimination far beyond its scope, effectively sanctioning abuse; LGBTQ+ Nigerians report lost job prospects and attacks have increased since the law passed. For this record: a decade-outcome assessment of the national criminalisation law, not just its text.

Context/Thomson Reuters Foundation (Apr 2024): 'kito' gangs entrap LGBTQ+ Nigerians via Grindr and other apps — victims lured to meetings then beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing; community counters with exposure forums (one admin's alert page drawing 43,000 followers) and sting operations. For this record: documented app-based luring crime specifically targeting queer people, relevant to a visitor using dating apps.

UK Home Office CPIN on Nigeria (June 2025, updated April 2026): same-sex sex between men is criminalised under secular law with up to 14 years' imprisonment; Sharia law in all 12 northern states criminalises same-sex acts between men and women, with male sodomy carrying the death penalty under state Zina provisions. For this record: current official UK-government assessment of penalties, including the north/Sharia overlay.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 401); the underlying Reuters report (Sept 2022) covers transgender Nigerians fearing proposals to criminalise cross-dressing.

records.name: Romania
records.summary:
Romania is broadly workable with a conservative political climate and significant legal-protection gaps, but a landmark EU court ruling and active civil society provide some positive trajectory. The European Court of Justice ruled in 2024 that Romania must recognize gender-identity changes made in other EU member states (the Mirin case), and a Romanian court definitively confirmed this in March 2026. Bucharest Pride marked its 20th anniversary with tens of thousands of marchers.

However, domestic legal gender recognition is court-based, restrictive, and inconsistently implemented. The anti-discrimination law does not explicitly cover gender identity (it covers "sex" and "sexual orientation" only), and the hate-crime law's aggravating-circumstance provision has never been applied in SOGIESC cases. No same-sex marriage or civil unions are recognised (the Orthodox Church successfully opposed reform). Far-right influences rose during the 2024-2025 election cycle, with anti-LGBTI rhetoric "intensified and repeatedly instrumentalised for political mobilisation."

ACCEPT Romania (31 Mar 2026): the Sector 6 Court of Bucharest ordered a new birth certificate for trans man Arian Mirzarafie-Ahi reflecting his UK-recognised identity, and the ruling became definitive after the Bucharest Tribunal rejected appeals filed by the Cluj civil-status directorates — building on the CJEU's 2024 ruling that member states must transcribe intra-EU legal gender recognition. Announced on Trans Day of Visibility; ACCEPT urges others who changed documents in another EU country to pursue transcription in Romania.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2026 (covering Jan–Dec 2025): anti-LGBTI rhetoric intensified during the 2025 presidential campaign — candidate Călin Georgescu declared himself 'against LGBTQ' in February and PM Ciolacu mocked gender-marker changes; the National Audiovisual Council issued a public warning to B1 TV in August over anti-Pride 'provocation' framing after an ACCEPT complaint; a Ploiești deputy mayor of AUR made further derogatory announcements.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2024 (covering 2023): the CNCD investigated printing houses that refused to print LGBT and gender-equality materials; the IPSOS PRIDE 2023 survey found 51% of Romanians agree same-sex families should enjoy legal recognition; March 2024 education-law drafts carried anti-discrimination provisions that drew 13 religious groups' protests and a 50+ organisation counter-response.

Outright International Romania overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): same-sex relations legal nationwide; GO 137/2000 covers sex and sexual orientation but institutional follow-through is limited; no marriage or civil unions (the 2018 constitution-ban referendum failed on low turnout; the Orthodox Church has opposed a civil-partnership bill since 2017); legal gender recognition possible; LGBTI organisations can register.

Council of Europe thematic review (Jan 2023): 'Hate Crimes and Other Hate Motivated Incidents Against LGBTI People in Romania' - national report on implementation of Recommendation CM/Rec(2010)5, covering legal/policy frameworks, applicable ECtHR case-law and international standards.

ILGA-Europe and partners' submission to the EU 2025 Rule of Law Report (2025), with ACCEPT Romania authoring the Romania chapter (p.29): of nine country submissions, eight reported smear campaigns, disinformation and hate speech against LGBTI people — the surge in anti-LGBTI narratives during the Romanian election period is cited as the clearest example of rights-impacting rule-of-law erosion.
AP (Jun 2025): 'Bucharest gay pride march turns 20 as LGBTQ+ Romanians face growing hostility' — tens of thousands march on the 20th anniversary amid rising right-wing hostility.
